subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia with coagulopathy and a raised urate at thirty six weeks
stem:
A 31 year old woman in her first pregnancy presents at 36 weeks with five days of nausea, vomiting and upper abdominal discomfort, and two days of feeling confused and unusually thirsty.

Her blood pressure has been normal at every antenatal visit including today, and her urine shows no protein. She is jaundiced. Her blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L despite eating this morning and has required a dextrose infusion. Her international normalised ratio is prolonged with a low fibrinogen, and her platelet count is only mildly reduced. Her haemoglobin is stable with no fragments on the film and her lactate dehydrogenase is only modestly raised. Foetal monitoring shows a reactive trace with normal growth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced, mildly encephalopathic with asterixis, tender right upper quadrant, no peripheral oedema, no hyperreflexia or clonus
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), international normalised ratio 2.1 (0.8-1.2), fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (2.0-4.5 in pregnancy), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), bilirubin 92 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 380 U/L (less than 35), urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90), no red cell fragments on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start magnesium sulfate and manage her expectantly
options.rationale: Magnesium is used for seizure prophylaxis in pre eclampsia, but her blood pressure is normal with no proteinuria and no hyperreflexia, and expectant management in this condition allows liver failure to progress. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan birth at 37 weeks
options.rationale: That approach belongs to intrahepatic cholestasis, which causes pruritus with raised bile acids but does not produce hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, encephalopathy or renal impairment. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Start plasma exchange for a thrombotic microangiopathy
options.rationale: Thrombotic microangiopathy is suggested by marked thrombocytopenia with red cell fragments, a falling haemoglobin and a high lactate dehydrogenase, none of which is present, and her film shows no fragments. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stabilise her and expedite the birth on the same day
options.rationale: Hypoglycaemia with early coagulopathy, hyperuricaemia, renal impairment and encephalopathy in the third trimester indicates acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and the only effective treatment is delivery, which should follow correction of glucose and coagulopathy without prolonged delay. Expectant management allows progression to fulminant hepatic failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange viral hepatitis serology before any decision
options.rationale: Serology should be sent but takes time to return, and viral hepatitis does not typically cause profound hypoglycaemia with hyperuricaemia in late pregnancy. Waiting for the result delays the only definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but rapidly progressive microvesicular steatosis of the third trimester that carries substantial maternal and perinatal mortality if delivery is delayed. The feature that most reliably distinguishes it from the overlapping syndrome of haemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelets is hypoglycaemia, which reflects loss of hepatic synthetic function and is not a feature of pre eclampsia related liver disease. Coagulopathy with a low fibrinogen appears early and out of proportion to the platelet count, and hyperuricaemia, renal impairment and encephalopathy are common. Treatment is stabilisation of glucose and clotting followed by prompt delivery, with intensive care support and readiness to manage postpartum haemorrhage.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia is the single most useful discriminator from the haemolysis and low platelet syndrome
Coagulopathy with low fibrinogen occurs early and is disproportionate to the thrombocytopenia
Blood pressure and urinalysis can be entirely normal
Delivery is the treatment; the liver recovers afterwards in most women
explanation.pearls: Test the infant for long chain 3 hydroxyacyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency afterwards: a foetal fatty acid oxidation defect underlies a proportion of cases, and identifying it protects that child and informs counselling for future pregnancies.

subtopic_detail: Failure of lactation and fatigue after a major obstetric haemorrhage
stem:
A 29 year old woman attends your clinic ten weeks after a birth complicated by a 3 litre postpartum haemorrhage that required six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in theatre.

She has never produced more than a few drops of milk despite intensive lactation support and has now stopped trying. She is profoundly tired, feels cold all the time and has not had a period. She has lost 4 kg without trying and describes feeling lightheaded when she stands up quickly. She is not breastfeeding, is taking no medication and her mood, while flat, does not meet criteria for a depressive episode on your assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, loss of axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation, no breast engorgement
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (10-25), thyroid stimulating hormone 0.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 9 am cortisol 62 nmol/L (185-624), prolactin low, follicle stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone both low
data_table.Obstetric history: Postpartum haemorrhage of 3 litres with transfusion and intraoperative hypotension

lead_in: What is the most important immediate treatment?

options.text: Start thyroxine replacement and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Thyroxine given before glucocorticoid accelerates cortisol metabolism and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in someone whose reserve is already exhausted, which is the specific danger in combined pituitary failure. Her thyroid deficiency is real but must be treated second. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start fludrocortisone for the postural drop in blood pressure
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid replacement is needed in primary adrenal failure, where the whole adrenal cortex is lost. In pituitary failure the renin angiotensin aldosterone axis is intact, so glucocorticoid alone is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline to correct her sodium concentration
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia here is a consequence of cortisol deficiency impairing free water excretion and corrects with glucocorticoid replacement. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start an antidepressant and arrange perinatal mental health review
options.rationale: Fatigue, flat affect and failure to establish breastfeeding invite a psychiatric explanation, but the biochemistry demonstrates a structural endocrine cause, and treating the mood alone leaves a potentially fatal cortisol deficiency untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start hydrocortisone replacement before any other hormone
options.rationale: A low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal thyroid stimulating hormone, low gonadotrophins, low prolactin with failed lactation and a 9 am cortisol of 62 nmol/L after a major obstetric haemorrhage indicates panhypopituitarism from pituitary infarction. Glucocorticoid is replaced first because starting thyroxine into untreated adrenal insufficiency can precipitate a crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Pituitary infarction following major obstetric haemorrhage produces panhypopituitarism, classically announced by failure of lactation because prolactin is lost early, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and postural hypotension. The biochemical signature is deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary axes with inappropriately normal or low trophic hormones, so a low free thyroxine sits alongside a thyroid stimulating hormone that is not raised. The sequencing of replacement is the critical clinical point: glucocorticoid must be given before thyroxine, because thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and can tip an already depleted patient into adrenal crisis. Mineralocorticoid is not required because aldosterone production is under renin control rather than pituitary control.
key_points: Failure of lactation after major haemorrhage is the earliest and most specific clue
A low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates central rather than primary hypothyroidism
Glucocorticoid always precedes thyroxine in suspected combined deficiency
Fludrocortisone is unnecessary because the renin angiotensin aldosterone axis is preserved
explanation.pearls: The absence of hyperpigmentation is a useful discriminator: in primary adrenal failure high adrenocorticotrophic hormone darkens skin creases and scars, whereas in pituitary failure the hormone is low and the patient looks pale rather than tanned.

subtopic_detail: Sudden collapse with coagulopathy moments after artificial rupture of membranes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite of a tertiary hospital. A 34 year old woman at 39 weeks is being augmented in labour and you have just performed an artificial rupture of membranes.

Within two minutes she says she feels strange and cannot breathe, becomes acutely agitated, then loses consciousness. She has no pulse. There is no external bleeding at this point and the uterus is well contracted. She has no known allergy, no cardiac history, and had received no new medication in the preceding hour other than the oxytocin infusion already running. The foetal heart rate falls to 60 beats per minute. Blood taken as access is established shows a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L and a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse absent, blood pressure unrecordable, respiratory effort absent, SpO2 unrecordable, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 60 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive with no palpable central pulse, uterus well contracted, no external haemorrhage, no urticaria, no angioedema, no bronchospasm audible
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5 in pregnancy), international normalised ratio markedly prolonged, platelets falling
data_table.Timing: Collapse within two minutes of artificial rupture of membranes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Begin resuscitation with left uterine displacement and prepare for birth
options.rationale: This is cardiac arrest in a pregnant woman, so chest compressions with manual left uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression begin immediately, and perimortem caesarean section should be performed within about four minutes if there is no return of circulation because it improves both maternal and neonatal survival. The early disproportionate coagulopathy points to amniotic fluid embolism, and massive transfusion with fibrinogen replacement is activated in parallel. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline and treat as anaphylaxis to oxytocin
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis is worth considering in any peripartum collapse, but the absence of urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm together with early profound coagulopathy points elsewhere, and adrenaline alone does not address the cardiac arrest. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy)

options.text: Give a fluid bolus and transfuse red cells for concealed haemorrhage
options.rationale: Concealed abruption is an important cause of peripartum collapse, but the uterus is well contracted and soft tissue bleeding is absent, and volume alone will not restore circulation in cardiac arrest. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous thrombolysis for a presumed pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is considered for confirmed or strongly suspected massive pulmonary embolism, but giving it to a woman who is already profoundly coagulopathic and about to undergo surgery would be catastrophic. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the oxytocin infusion and reassess her over the next few minutes
options.rationale: Stopping the infusion is a reasonable simultaneous action but observing a woman in cardiac arrest for a few minutes forfeits the interval during which resuscitation and perimortem caesarean can save her. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is rare but is a leading direct cause of maternal death, and it characteristically presents as sudden cardiorespiratory collapse during labour, at rupture of membranes or immediately after birth, often with a premonitory sense of doom or agitation. What distinguishes it from other causes of peripartum collapse is the early and profound disseminated intravascular coagulation, with fibrinogen falling out of proportion to any blood loss. There is no diagnostic test in the acute setting and the diagnosis is clinical. Management is high quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation with manual left uterine displacement, perimortem caesarean within about four minutes if circulation does not return, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy with fibrinogen replacement through a massive transfusion protocol.
key_points: Early coagulopathy out of proportion to bleeding is the feature that separates it from other causes of collapse
Manual left uterine displacement rather than a tilted position is used during compressions
Perimortem caesarean within about four minutes improves both maternal and neonatal survival
Diagnosis is clinical; no confirmatory test is available in time to guide management
explanation.pearls: Perimortem caesarean is a maternal resuscitative manoeuvre first and a neonatal one second: emptying the uterus relieves aortocaval compression and can restore maternal cardiac output, which is why it is indicated even when the foetus is not expected to survive.

sources.label: ANZCOR: Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in special circumstances
